proposals.text: Carts must not be taken into single-file shelf aisles.
proposals.justification: The rule is defined by aisle width and shelf adjacency, so it applies to any store layout with narrow shelf aisles rather than to particular coordinates.

proposals.text: A shopper must not enter a single-file shelf aisle while still holding a cart.
proposals.justification: The prohibited transition is described in terms of moving into a narrow shelf-flanked passage, which is a layout-independent spatial relation.

proposals.text: Carts may only be pushed through aisles that are wide enough for carts.
proposals.justification: The constraint depends on local free-space width rather than named cells, so the same norm can be evaluated in stores with different floor plans.

proposals.text: If a shopper temporarily leaves a cart, the cart should be left in a wide circulation area away from shelves.
proposals.justification: The allowed parking location is characterized by usable open space and lack of shelf adjacency, not by a specific parking coordinate.

proposals.text: A shopper must not select or interact with shelf goods in a single-file shelf aisle while holding a cart.
proposals.justification: The rule concerns the general situation of handling goods in a narrow shelf aisle, independent of where that aisle is located.

proposals.text: After selecting an item on foot inside a single-file shelf aisle, the shopper must reclaim their cart before leaving the store.
proposals.justification: The obligation is triggered by a layout-independent activity pattern—leaving the cart to shop in a narrow shelf aisle—rather than by visiting a named cell.

proposals.text: A shopper should obtain a cart during the shopping trip before exiting.
proposals.justification: Cart possession is a general shopping-domain condition and does not depend on the position or geometry of any particular store.

proposals.text: A shopper must not leave the store without their cart.
proposals.justification: The exit rule refers only to the general act of leaving with or without a cart, so it remains meaningful across different store layouts.

The demonstrations are now shown in a lower-level representation that exposes distinctions hidden before (newly available: geometry). Identify the hidden distinctions and use them to define higher-level state properties and/or events (in "abstraction"), possibly hierarchically, and propose norms expressed over them. Norms may also use the primitive atoms directly.
Generalisation requirement. Some candidate rules merely describe the particular store in which the demonstrations were recorded -- for example rules that mention specific coordinates, cells or regions of this floor plan. Such rules can fit the demonstrations without capturing the social norm, and would be meaningless in a store with a different floor plan. Distinguish (a) candidate norms that express general behavioural constraints of the shopping domain from (b) rules that only describe the geometry or coordinates of this particular environment. Propose candidates of type (a): define any abstractions from layout-independent relations rather than from coordinates (at(x,y)), so that the same rule could be applied unchanged in any store layout. Every candidate must still be consistent with all demonstrations. Add a field "justification" (one sentence) to each element explaining why the rule remains meaningful across different store layouts.
Propose 8 diverse candidate hypotheses.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON list (no prose, no code fences). Each element:
{"id": short_name, "text": one-sentence natural-language statement of the norm,
 "abstraction": {"state_properties": {name: FORMULA, ...},
                 "events": {name: {"pre": FORMULA, "post": FORMULA or null}, ...}},
 "norm": {"type": "prohibition", "condition": FORMULA}
       | {"type": "obligation", "trigger": FORMULA or "START", "discharge": FORMULA}}
FORMULA := atom | name of a property/event defined in this hypothesis | {"not": F} | {"and": [F, ...]}
         | {"or": [F, ...]} | {"le"|"lt"|"ge"|"gt"|"eq": [numeric_feature, integer]}
Semantics.  A trajectory is a sequence of steps (state s_k, action a_k).  A step's label contains the atoms true in
s_k and the action a_k.  A state property is a formula over state atoms (no actions).  An event
{"pre": P, "post": Q} occurs at step k when P holds for the label of step k and Q holds in the next state s_{k+1}
(post may be null).  A prohibition counts one violation for every step whose label (including events occurring at
that step) satisfies the condition.  An obligation becomes pending at any step satisfying the trigger ("START" =
pending from the beginning) and is fulfilled by a later (or the same) step satisfying the discharge; it can be
triggered again; it is violated if it is still pending when the trajectory ends.

parsed.text: If a shopper temporarily leaves a cart, the cart should be left in a wide circulation area away from shelves.
parsed.justification: The allowed parking location is characterized by usable open space and lack of shelf adjacency, not by a specific parking coordinate.

parsed.text: A shopper must not select or interact with shelf goods in a single-file shelf aisle while holding a cart.
parsed.justification: The rule concerns the general situation of handling goods in a narrow shelf aisle, independent of where that aisle is located.

parsed.text: After selecting an item on foot inside a single-file shelf aisle, the shopper must reclaim their cart before leaving the store.
parsed.justification: The obligation is triggered by a layout-independent activity pattern—leaving the cart to shop in a narrow shelf aisle—rather than by visiting a named cell.

parsed.text: A shopper should obtain a cart during the shopping trip before exiting.
parsed.justification: Cart possession is a general shopping-domain condition and does not depend on the position or geometry of any particular store.

parsed.text: A shopper must not leave the store without their cart.
parsed.justification: The exit rule refers only to the general act of leaving with or without a cart, so it remains meaningful across different store layouts.
